draft.title: Evaluation reveals values
card: Evaluation is when a writer judges something as good or bad, important or trivial, right or wrong. Writers do it all the time, often without saying so.
the writer states the opinion in plain words, such as 'This is a wonderful park'.
the writer suggests an opinion through word choice, such as 'The park is a patch of weeds the council forgot'. The words 'patch of weeds' and 'forgot' carry the judgement.
A judgement shows what the writer values. Praising a quiet park suggests the writer values calm. Mocking a fast food ad may suggest they value health or honesty.
draft.remember: Ask what a writer is judging, and what that judgement says they care about.

a.q: A writer says a town's new library is a bold, welcoming space that opens doors for every child. What does this evaluation suggest the writer values?
opts: Access to learning for everyone
Saving money on public buildings
Keeping the town's old buildings
Making the town look modern
a.why: The words welcoming, opens doors and every child show the writer values learning that all children can reach. Modern looks are not the focus of the judgement, even though bold might hint at design.
a.clue: Look at which words praise the library, and what they have in common.

b.q: Dev writes: 'The council tore up the old oval for yet another car park.' Which statement best describes how this sentence evaluates the council's choice?
opts: It hints at disapproval through the words 'yet another'
It openly states that the council was wrong
It gives a neutral report with no judgement
It praises the council for meeting a local need
b.why: The writer never says 'wrong' or 'bad', but 'tore up' and 'yet another' hint at disapproval and suggest a value for green space. It is not neutral, because those word choices carry a judgement. It is hinted rather than open.
b.clue: Does the writer use a plain opinion word, or hint through other words?

b.best: It hints at disapproval through the words 'yet another'

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that quotes a precise detail from the sentence ('yet another') and is the longest, so a student could pick it without understanding hinted judgement.
